research_concepts: design validation for detecting offensive unit influence
methodological_questions: Can we isolate the effect of changing only the offensive five while holding the defensive five constant?
What is the natural game-to-game and stint-to-stint variability in shot mix for a fixed offensive unit?
How many possessions are needed per stint for reliable shot-mix estimation?
How to control for game-state confounders (score, time, period, opponent, fatigue) when comparing stints?
Is the effect size of a personnel change on shot mix large enough to be detected with available sample sizes?
What statistical test (global distributional difference) is most appropriate and robust to low-frequency shot types?
evidence_establishes: No historical evidence was available; the retrieval returned zero records.
evidence_does_not_establish: No prior work from this project has tested whether an offensive-only substitution changes shot mix, nor validated the design for detecting personnel-driven effects on shot distribution.
own_inferences: The question can be reframed as a validation study: if the data infrastructure can detect a shift in shot distribution when the offensive unit changes (defense held constant), it demonstrates sensitivity to personnel effects.
The primary confound is simultaneous defensive substitutions; these must be filtered out to isolate the offensive effect.
Shot mix must be operationalized as a multinomial distribution over shot-type categories derivable from play-by-play actionType/subType and shot distance.
A paired pre-post substitution comparison within the same game and same defensive unit provides a within-game control, mitigating many between-game confounds.
Stints with very few possessions will produce noisy shot-mix estimates, requiring minimum-possession filters that reduce sample size but improve reliability.
A permutation-based null distribution, built from periods where the offensive five did not change (placebo), can assess whether observed shifts exceed natural variability.

Three seasons of data (2022-23 through 2024-25) likely provide adequate statistical power if the effect is modest, but power will be limited by the number of offense-only substitutions with sufficient possessions.
uncertainties: The magnitude of any true personnel-driven shift in shot mix is unknown; the effect could be too small to detect even with the full dataset.

The exact definition of 'shot mix' is not specified in the prompt; it could refer to shot distance categories, shot type (e.g., jump shot, layup), or even play-type mix derived from the graph database, which would change the analysis.
It is unclear whether the study intends to test a single global hypothesis or explore individual player/lineup effects, which would inflate multiplicity.
The extent to which offensive substitutions occur without a corresponding defensive change is unknown; filtering could severely reduce event counts.
Game-state influences (e.g., end-of-shot-clock heaves, intentional fouls) might confound pre-post comparisons if not carefully addressed.

historical_effect.explanation: No historical evidence was available to influence the decision; the assessment relies solely on the research question, available data, and general methodological considerations.

blocking_constraints.text: The number of offense-only substitutions (defensive five unchanged) with sufficient possessions per stint may be too small to detect a modest effect, risking an underpowered null result.

Simultaneous defensive substitutions are a strong confound; unless filtered, any observed shot-mix change could be driven by the defense. Even when filtered, residual confounds from game state (score, time, period, opponent tactics) may remain.
Shot-type classification from play-by-play may have misclassifications, particularly for ambiguous action types, adding noise that could obscure a true signal.
Some shot-type categories (e.g., dunks, non-paint 2s) occur infrequently; their proportions will be estimated with high variance, potentially destabilizing a multivariate test.

prior_work.summary: No earlier studies on this specific question were retrieved by the system; it is unknown whether similar validation has been attempted internally.

risks.text: Filtering to offense-only substitutions with at least N possessions pre and post may leave a small number of events, reducing power to detect a true shift in shot mix.
Unobserved game-state variables (e.g., defensive scheme adjustment, player fatigue, score differential) influence shot selection and may co-vary with the decision to substitute.
Play-by-play action descriptions can be inconsistent across arenas and seasons; inferring shot categories (e.g., floaters vs. pull-ups) introduces measurement error.
Rare shot types (e.g., dunks, corner threes) produce zero-cell issues in stint-level distributions, complicating chi-squared or divergence measures.
Exploratory slicing by team, lineup, or specific personnel would inflate false positives unless a pre-registered global test is used and all other analyses are labeled secondary.
Defining 'pre' and 'post' stints using substitution time stamps must ensure that the possession containing the substitution is correctly assigned and not split in a way that leaks information.
If the analysis pools across an entire three-year period, long-term strategic trends in shot selection could masquerade as a personnel effect, though within-game comparisons mitigate this.

design.estimand: The difference in multinomial shot-type distribution between the final stint of an offensive five-man unit and the immediately following first stint of a new offensive five-man unit, when the defensive five remains constant.
design.unit: A pair of contiguous stints (pre-substitution, post-substitution) within the same game, same opponent, same defensive personnel.
design.sample: All regular-season games from the 2022-23, 2023-24, and 2024-25 NBA seasons. Exclude garbage time (Q4 minutes when the absolute score difference exceeds 20 points) and any period where possession data is incomplete. Include only substitution events where (a) the offensive team changes exactly the players on the floor, (b) the defensive team makes no substitution between those two stints, (c) each stint contains at least 5 offensive possessions for that team. Duplicate events (e.g., staggered multi-player subs) will be collapsed into one transition. The resulting dataset will be cleaned to remove events where the substitution was likely due to injury or foul trouble (manually identify if description available, otherwise retain but note).
design.power: We will compute observed effect size using a pre-registered pilot from the 2022-23 season only. If the effect size (Cramer's V or earth mover's distance) is non-zero, we will estimate the minimum number of events N needed for 80% power at alpha=0.05 using a paired permutation test. We will then verify that the remaining two seasons provide at least 1.2×N events; if not, we will pool all three seasons and report achieved power. The primary analysis will be on the holdout set (2023-24 and 2024-25) if the pilot sets a threshold; otherwise, a pooled analysis with adjusted significance.
design.controls: Primary confound control is the requirement that the defensive five does not change. Additional controls: include fixed effects for game (to absorb opponent and venue), period, and the interaction of period and score margin (binned). Sensitivity analyses will exclude the first possession after a substitution (to allow the offense to set up) and weight possessions by the time left on the shot clock to account for end-of-clock desperation shots. We will also report results stratified by whether the substitution was a single-player change or a full-lineup swap (multiple players), as effect magnitudes may differ.
design.falsification: We will construct a placebo distribution by randomly pairing stints where the offensive five remained unchanged (same 10 players) and computing the same shot-mix difference statistic. The observed distribution for actual substitutions should be significantly larger (one-tailed test). Additionally, we will test the null of no effect using a permutation test that randomly reassigns the 'pre' and 'post' labels within each event. Both tests must be satisfied to claim a detectable shift.
design.multiplicity: The primary hypothesis is a single global test of distributional inequality (energy statistic or chi-squared). No family-wise adjustment is required. Any per-player or per-lineup analyses will be clearly labeled as secondary and will use false discovery rate control.
design.decision_rule: We reject the null of no shift in shot mix if the p-value from the permutation test (comparing actual pre-post differences to the placebo null distribution) is below 0.05. To conclude the design can detect personnel effects, we require a statistically significant shift and an effect size (Cramer's V) above a pre-registered minimum of 0.05 (small but non-zero). If the null is retained, we will assess achieved power; if low, the result is inconclusive.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files as of 2026-11-02: pbp, rotation, matchups, summary, starters for 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25 seasons. Derived play-type possession records from the project's graph database will be used only for descriptive correlation with shot mix; the primary analysis uses raw pbp shot actions.

methodological_questions: measurement reliability of shot type classification

Additionally, we should think about risk codes. Potential risks:
- SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER: number of lineup-change events where the offensive five changes and enough possessions on both sides to estimate shot mix? The offensive five changes frequently; there might be many substitutions, but the shot mix may require many possessions to get reliable distribution. If we compare per stint, stints can be short.
- EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: some five-man lineups are rarely used, so the change events for certain personnel combinations may be sparse, but the overall question might just test the general phenomenon of "changing the offensive five moves shot mix" without focusing on specific lineups; we could pool across all changes, testing whether the distribution differs before vs after. TOOL_RESULT glossary:
# Terminology used in the research questions

This glossary is given identically in every condition. It defines terms only and reports no results. Definitions follow the published papers (Structural Influence; Detecting Defensive Suppression) where they exist.

- **Possession, PPP:** a team's continuous spell with the ball; PPP is points per possession.
- **H1, H2:** first half (periods 1 and 2) and second half (periods 3 and 4) of a game. RS and PO: regular season and playoffs.
- **Play type:** the label assigned to each possession by the project's rule-based classifier from play-by-play events. Labels include PNR (pick-and-roll ball handler), DRIVE, CUT, SPOT_UP, PULL_UP, POST_UP, PUTBACK and TRANSITION. A play-type mix is a team's share of possessions in each play type.
- **Initiator, initiation:** the offensive player whose action starts the possession's play type (for example the cutter on a cut, the ball handler on a pick-and-roll). Initiation records are possession-level rows linking initiator, play type and points.
- **Inferrer:** the classifier step that infers a play type (for example a pick-and-roll) from play-by-play text when it is not recorded directly.
- **Suppression trigger:** a team, play type and game in which the team's PPP on that play type falls sharply from H1 to H2 under fixed minimum-attempt rules; read as the defense possibly taking the action away.
- **Continuation, counter:** after a trigger, continuation means the offense keeps running the triggered play type; a counter is a different play type run instead.
- **BEST, AVOID (counter tiers):** the strategy app's matchup-ranked counter recommendations after a trigger. BEST is the top-ranked counter play type for that matchup, AVOID the lowest-ranked.
- **Structural fingerprint:** a team's standardized pattern of how play types share initiators.
- **Structural influence (load, L):** how much a team's structural fingerprint changes when one player's initiations are removed. L_pre is that quantity measured from games before an absence.
- **Usage:** a player's share of team possessions he initiates or finishes.
- **Role categories (Structural Influence paper):** by crossing usage (above or below the rotation median) with residual influence (structural influence beyond what usage predicts): Primary Organizer (high usage, positive residual), Shaper (low usage, positive residual), Terminal Scorer (high usage, residual at or below zero), Role Occupant or Specialist (low usage, residual at or below zero).
- **Connector:** a structural-role label used in later studies for players whose presence links teammates' play types; the exact rule varied between studies.
- **Hub:** a high-structural-influence player around whom a team's initiations are organized.
- **Absence spell:** a run of consecutive games a player misses (the main studies used at least 15).
- **Displacement (D_real):** how far teammates' play-type mix moves during an absence spell relative to before it (one minus the cosine similarity of the two mixes).
- **Mover, decoy:** a mover is a player who changed teams between seasons; decoys are comparison players used as placebo matches for a mover.
- **Stint:** an interval of play with the same ten players on the court.
- **Garbage time:** late-game possessions with a lopsided score, usually excluded.

We have completed the retrieval stage, which returned 0 results. Now Stage 2 begins. We need to follow steps 4-9 and produce the final output object. Since no historical evidence is available, we must base our assessment on the research question, data, tools, and our own reasoning. Let's first list the research concepts and methodological questions we identified in stage 1 (already in the retrieval call). We'll then assess testability, risks, predicted outcomes, and design.

Research question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects." Data: NBA 2022-23 to 2024-25 regular season and playoffs, per-game files with pbp, rotation, matchups, summary, starters, plus derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database. So we have play-by-play and derived play types (possession-level). The question is about shot mix. "Shot mix" presumably refers to the distribution of shot types (like shot type categories: 2pt jumpers, 3pt, at-rim, etc.). The pbp includes actionType, subType, shotDistance, etc., so shot types can be derived. The question: "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects." It seems like a validation study: if we compare stints where the offensive five players are the same vs. when they change (due to substitution), does the shot mix shift? If so, that shows the design (presumably the data infrastructure and analysis) can detect personnel-driven effects. This is essentially testing whether the methodology is sensitive enough to detect changes in shot distribution attributable to different on-court units.

We need to decide if this can be answered with the data. Let's identify methodological risks: 
- SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER: number of substitution events where the offensive five changes and then a subsequent stint with the new five occurs, with enough possessions to estimate shot mix reliably. We need to consider the sparsity of unique five-man lineups; many substitutions involve only one player change. We could focus on stints immediately after a substitution, comparing shot mix in this stint vs. previous stint. But the number of possessions per stint may be small. The data includes per-game files, but we can aggregate across games. However, we must define the unit of analysis: a contiguous stint with the same ten players. The research question could be operationalized as: For each game, for each substitution that changes the offensive five, compare the distribution of shot types (or play types?) in the N possessions before the substitution vs. the N possessions after, controlling for opponent defense (the defensive five might also change). The question says "Changing the offensive five itself moves shot mix, showing the design can detect personnel effects." So they might want to isolate offensive personnel changes while holding defense constant, or they might accept that defensive changes co-occur. This leads to CONFOUNDING: if the offensive five changes, often the defensive five also changes (substitutions often involve both teams). So any change in shot mix could be due to the new defensive unit rather than the offensive personnel change. To show that the design can detect personnel effects, we might need to control for defense. Could we use matchups data? The matchups file gives defensive matchup minutes per game, but not possession-level. However, we could use the stint information from rotation data to know which ten players are on court. We could restrict to cases where only the offensive team makes a substitution, while the defensive five remains unchanged. That is possible: one team calls a sub, the other doesn't. In that case, the defensive personnel stays the same. Then we can compare shot mix in stints before and after the offensive sub, with the same defensive unit. That would isolate offensive personnel change. That reduces confound, but reduces sample size as many subs are simultaneous.

- EXPOSURE_SPARSITY: Even with same defense, the number of such events might be small. Also, we need enough possessions to measure shot mix reliably. Shot mix proportions with small samples can be noisy. Power might be low.

- MEASURE_RELIABILITY: shot type classification. The pbp has actionType/subType (e.g., jump shot, layup, dunk, three point). Might be reliable. Play-type possession records could also be used. But "shot mix" probably refers to shot types, not play types. We can define categories (at-rim, 2pt mid-range, 3pt, etc.) from distance and action type.

- OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL: the outcome is the shift in shot mix. What measure? Cosine distance, Euclidean distance, chi-squared? Not inherently derived from the outcome variable, but the label "personnel effect" is not being predicted; we're just testing if there is a shift.

- LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD: Using play-by-play to define stints before/after substitution, we need to ensure no lookahead bias (i.e., using future events to classify shot mix of a stint). That can be avoided by proper segmentation.

- MECHANICAL_FLOOR: Some shot types have zero frequency in certain stints, causing infinite odds ratios or issues.

- BASE_RATE: Some shot types are rare (e.g., dunks). Could cause instability.

- CONFOUNDING: defensive changes, as said. Also, substitution may be related to game state (score, time remaining), which could affect shot selection (e.g., end-of-quarter heaves, garbage time). Need to control for game context (period, score difference, clock). Garbage time can be excluded.

- MULTIPLE_TESTING: If we test many individual shot type proportions, we need to adjust. But the primary hypothesis is a global measure of difference in distribution.

- DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY: Over seasons, shot selection trends may change, but we're comparing stints within the same game, so stationarity should hold.

- IMPLEMENTATION_BUG: data processing errors.

- PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE: could do placebo test: comparing two stints with the same offensive five (no change) to see if shot mix differs randomly, as a null distribution.

Now, testability: I'd say it is testable, but with challenges. Probability of useful power is moderate, given the large number of games across three seasons. Let's estimate p_testable: 0.7. Blocking constraints: maybe sample size power, confounding.

Prior work: we retrieved none, so already_answered = "unknown". historical_evidence and failed_approaches are empty lists.

Now design: We need a pre-registration-quality design.

Estimand: The expected change in shot distribution (multivariate) when the offensive five changes, holding the defensive five constant, compared to random variation when the offensive five remains unchanged.

Unit: A possession or a stint (aggregate). I think stint-level: compare the distribution of possessions in the stint immediately before the substitution to that in the stint immediately after, excluding the first few possessions of the new stint to allow for settling?
